stem: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
solution: **Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** is the amount of the filtrate formed by the kidneys per minute. In a healthy individual it is approximately **125 ml/minute**, i.e., about **180 litres per day**.
groundedIn: §16.2 — the amount of the filtrate formed by the kidneys per minute is GFR; approximately 125 ml/minute, i.e., 180 litres per day

stem: Explain the autoregulatory mechanism of GFR.
solution:
The kidneys regulate their own GFR mainly through the **juxta glomerular apparatus (JGA)**, by the **renin-angiotensin mechanism**.

1. **JGA** is a special sensitive region formed by cellular modifications in the **distal convoluted tubule** and the **afferent arteriole** at the location of their contact.
2. A fall in glomerular blood flow, glomerular blood pressure or GFR activates the **JG cells** to release **renin**.
3. Renin converts **angiotensinogen** in blood to **angiotensin I** and further to **angiotensin II**.
4. Angiotensin II, a powerful **vasoconstrictor**, increases the glomerular blood pressure and thereby the GFR.
5. Angiotensin II also activates the **adrenal cortex** to release **aldosterone**, which causes reabsorption of \(\text{Na}^+\) and water from the distal parts of the tubule. This also increases blood pressure and GFR.
6. In this way the glomerular blood flow, and with it the GFR, is brought back to normal.
7. An increase in blood flow to the atria releases **Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF)**, which causes vasodilation and decreases blood pressure; ANF acts as a check on the renin-angiotensin mechanism.
groundedIn: §16.2; §16.5 — JGA formed by modifications of DCT and afferent arteriole; a fall in GFR activates JG cells to release renin, bringing GFR back to normal; renin-angiotensin mechanism, aldosterone, and ANF as a check

context: Indicate whether the following statements are true or false :
stem: Micturition is carried out by a reflex.
solution: **True.** Micturition is carried out by the **micturition reflex**. Stretch receptors on the walls of the filling urinary bladder send signals to the CNS, which passes on motor messages that contract the smooth muscles of the bladder and relax the urethral sphincter, releasing urine.
groundedIn: §16.6 — the neural mechanism causing the release of urine is called the micturition reflex

context: Indicate whether the following statements are true or false :
stem: ADH helps in water elimination, making the urine hypotonic.
solution:
**False.** ADH (antidiuretic hormone or vasopressin) facilitates water **reabsorption** from the latter parts of the tubule and so prevents diuresis.

Corrected statement: ADH helps in water reabsorption, making the urine concentrated (hypertonic).
groundedIn: §16.5 — ADH facilitates water reabsorption from latter parts of the tubule, thereby preventing diuresis

context: Indicate whether the following statements are true or false :
stem: Protein-free fluid is filtered from blood plasma into the Bowman's capsule.
solution: **True.** Glomerular filtration is an **ultra filtration**. Blood is filtered through the endothelium of the glomerular blood vessels, the basement membrane and the epithelium of Bowman's capsule (podocytes with filtration slits) so finely that almost all the constituents of the plasma **except the proteins** pass into the lumen of Bowman's capsule.
groundedIn: §16.2 — almost all the constituents of the plasma except the proteins pass onto the lumen of the Bowman's capsule; ultra filtration

subtopic: Mechanism of Concentration of the Filtrate
context: Indicate whether the following statements are true or false :
stem: Henle's loop plays an important role in concentrating the urine.
solution: **True.** Henle's loop, together with the vasa recta, sets up the **counter current mechanism**, which maintains an increasing osmolarity in the medullary interstitium (from 300 mOsmolL\(^{-1}\) in the cortex to about 1200 mOsmolL\(^{-1}\) in the inner medulla). This gradient allows easy passage of water from the collecting tubule, concentrating the urine.
groundedIn: §16.4 — Henle's loop and vasa recta play a significant role in producing a concentrated urine; counter current mechanism maintains the medullary gradient

context: Indicate whether the following statements are true or false :
stem: Glucose is actively reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.
solution: **True.** Glucose in the filtrate is reabsorbed **actively** by the tubular epithelial cells, and nearly all of the essential nutrients are reabsorbed in the **proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)**, whose simple cuboidal brush border epithelium increases the surface area for reabsorption.
groundedIn: §16.2; §16.3; Fig. 16.5 — glucose, amino acids, Na+ are reabsorbed actively; nearly all essential nutrients are reabsorbed in the PCT

subtopic: Mechanism of Concentration of the Filtrate
stem: Give a brief account of the counter current mechanism.
solution:
The **counter current mechanism** is the transport of NaCl and urea, facilitated by the special arrangement of **Henle's loop** and **vasa recta**, that maintains a concentration gradient in the medullary interstitium and so concentrates the urine.

1. The filtrate flows in opposite directions in the two limbs of Henle's loop, forming a **counter current**. Blood in the two limbs of the vasa recta also flows in a counter current pattern.
2. The proximity of Henle's loop and vasa recta, and the counter current in them, maintain an **increasing osmolarity** towards the inner medulla: from **300 mOsmolL\(^{-1}\)** in the cortex to about **1200 mOsmolL\(^{-1}\)** in the inner medulla.
3. The gradient is mainly caused by **NaCl and urea**.
4. NaCl transported by the ascending limb of Henle's loop is exchanged with the descending limb of vasa recta, and is returned to the interstitium by the ascending portion of vasa recta.
5. Small amounts of urea enter the thin segment of the ascending limb of Henle's loop and are transported back to the interstitium by the collecting tubule.
6. The descending limb (permeable to water, almost impermeable to electrolytes) concentrates the filtrate; the ascending limb (impermeable to water, transports electrolytes) dilutes it.
7. The interstitial gradient allows easy passage of water from the collecting tubule, so human kidneys can produce urine nearly **four times** as concentrated as the initial filtrate.
groundedIn: §16.4; §16.3; Fig. 16.6 — counter current in Henle's loop and vasa recta; 300 to 1200 mOsmolL-1 gradient caused by NaCl and urea; permeability of the two limbs; urine nearly four times concentrated

subtopic: Role of Other Organs in Excretion
stem: Describe the role of liver, lungs and skin in excretion.
solution:
Other than the kidneys, the **lungs, liver and skin** also help in the elimination of excretory wastes.

1. **Lungs** remove large amounts of \(\text{CO}_2\) (approximately 200 mL/minute) and also significant quantities of water every day.
2. **Liver**, the largest gland in the body, secretes **bile** containing substances like **bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins and drugs**. Most of these pass out along with the digestive wastes.
3. **Skin** eliminates certain substances through the secretions of its glands:
   - **Sweat glands** produce sweat, a watery fluid containing NaCl, small amounts of urea, lactic acid, etc. Its primary function is a cooling effect on the body surface, but it also removes these wastes.
   - **Sebaceous glands** eliminate substances like **sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes** through **sebum**, which also provides a protective oily covering for the skin.
groundedIn: §16.7 — lungs remove CO2 (about 200 mL/minute) and water; liver secretes bile with bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, steroid hormones, vitamins and drugs; sweat and sebaceous glands

stem: Explain micturition.
solution:
**Micturition** is the process of release of urine; the neural mechanism causing it is the **micturition reflex**.

1. Urine formed by the nephrons is carried to the **urinary bladder**, where it is stored till a voluntary signal is given by the **central nervous system (CNS)**.
2. As the bladder fills with urine it stretches, and **stretch receptors** on its walls send signals to the CNS.
3. The CNS passes on motor messages that initiate **contraction of the smooth muscles of the bladder** and simultaneous **relaxation of the urethral sphincter**.
4. This causes the release of urine through the urethra.

An adult human excretes, on an average, 1 to 1.5 litres of urine per day.
groundedIn: §16.6 — urine stored in the bladder till a voluntary CNS signal; stretch receptors; contraction of bladder smooth muscle and relaxation of urethral sphincter; micturition reflex

stem: What is meant by the term osmoregulation?
solution: **Osmoregulation** is the regulation of the **ionic and fluid volume** of the body fluids, i.e., the maintenance of their fluid and ionic balance. Excretory structures such as protonephridia (flame cells), nephridia and Malpighian tubules help in osmoregulation besides removing nitrogenous wastes.
groundedIn: §16.0 — protonephridia are primarily concerned with ionic and fluid volume regulation, i.e., osmoregulation; nephridia and Malpighian tubules maintain fluid and ionic balance

stem: Terrestrial animals are generally either ureotelic or uricotelic, not ammonotelic, why ?
solution:
Terrestrial animals have to **conserve water**, and ammonia cannot be eliminated without a large loss of water.

1. **Ammonia** is the most toxic nitrogenous waste and requires a **large amount of water** for its elimination. Being readily soluble, it is excreted by diffusion across body surfaces or gill surfaces, which suits aquatic animals.
2. Terrestrial adaptation therefore necessitated the production of **less toxic** nitrogenous wastes, **urea** and **uric acid**, for conservation of water.
3. **Ureotelic** animals (mammals, many terrestrial amphibians) convert ammonia into urea in the liver; the urea is filtered and excreted by the kidneys.
4. **Uricotelic** animals (reptiles, birds, land snails and insects) excrete **uric acid**, the least toxic form, as pellet or paste with a minimum loss of water.
groundedIn: §16.0 — ammonia most toxic, needs large amount of water; terrestrial adaptation necessitated lesser toxic urea and uric acid for conservation of water; ureotelic and uricotelic animals

stem: What is the significance of juxta glomerular apparatus (JGA) in kidney function?
solution:
The **juxta glomerular apparatus (JGA)** regulates the **glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** and blood pressure through the **renin-angiotensin mechanism**.

1. JGA is a special sensitive region formed by cellular modifications in the **distal convoluted tubule** and the **afferent arteriole** at the location of their contact.
2. A fall in glomerular blood flow, glomerular blood pressure or GFR activates the **JG cells** to release **renin**.
3. Renin converts angiotensinogen in blood to angiotensin I and further to **angiotensin II**, a powerful vasoconstrictor that increases glomerular blood pressure and thereby GFR.
4. Angiotensin II also activates the adrenal cortex to release **aldosterone**, which causes reabsorption of \(\text{Na}^+\) and water from the distal parts of the tubule, further increasing blood pressure and GFR.

Thus the JGA brings a fallen GFR back to normal.
groundedIn: §16.2; §16.5 — JGA is a special sensitive region of DCT and afferent arteriole; a fall in GFR activates JG cells to release renin; renin-angiotensin mechanism and aldosterone

stem: A chordate animal having flame cells as excretory structures
solution: **Amphioxus**, a cephalochordate, which has protonephridia or flame cells as its excretory structures.
groundedIn: §16.0 — protonephridia or flame cells are the excretory structures in Platyhelminthes, rotifers, some annelids and the cephalochordate Amphioxus

stem: Cortical portions projecting between the medullary pyramids in the human kidney
solution: **Columns of Bertini** (renal columns): the extensions of the cortex in between the medullary pyramids.
groundedIn: §16.1; Fig. 16.2 — the cortex extends in between the medullary pyramids as renal columns called Columns of Bertini

stem: A loop of capillary running parallel to the Henle's loop.
solution: **Vasa recta**: a minute vessel of the peritubular capillary network that runs parallel to Henle's loop, forming a 'U' shape.
groundedIn: §16.1; Fig. 16.3 — a minute vessel of the peritubular network runs parallel to the Henle's loop forming a U shaped vasa recta

stem: Ascending limb of Henle's loop is _______ to water whereas the descending limb is _______ to it.
solution:
**impermeable**; **permeable**

Ascending limb of Henle's loop is **impermeable** to water whereas the descending limb is **permeable** to it.
groundedIn: §16.3 — the descending limb is permeable to water; the ascending limb is impermeable to water

stem: Reabsorption of water from distal parts of the tubules is facilitated by hormone _______.
solution:
**ADH** (antidiuretic hormone or vasopressin)

Reabsorption of water from distal parts of the tubules is facilitated by hormone **ADH**.

ADH, released from the neurohypophysis, facilitates water reabsorption from the latter parts of the tubule and prevents diuresis. Aldosterone also causes reabsorption of \(\text{Na}^+\) and water from the distal parts of the tubule, but the hormone whose role is water reabsorption itself is ADH.
groundedIn: §16.5 — ADH facilitates water reabsorption from latter parts of the tubule; aldosterone causes reabsorption of Na+ and water from the distal parts

stem: Dialysis fluid contain all the constituents as in plasma except _______.
solution:
**nitrogenous wastes**

Dialysis fluid contain all the constituents as in plasma except **nitrogenous wastes**.

Because nitrogenous wastes are absent from the dialysing fluid, they move freely out of the blood across the porous cellophane membrane along the concentration gradient, clearing the blood.
groundedIn: §16.8 — the dialysing fluid has the same composition as that of plasma except the nitrogenous wastes

stem: A healthy adult human excretes (on an average) _______ gm of urea/day.
solution:
**25-30**

A healthy adult human excretes (on an average) **25-30** gm of urea/day.
groundedIn: §16.6 — on an average, 25-30 gm of urea is excreted out per day
